Create square or hexagonal grid polygons over a boundary

Source: R/tessellation.R
create_grid_polygons.Rd

Lays a regular grid of equal-area cells over boundary and clips it to that boundary. Use it rather than create_voronoi_polygons() when you set the cell size yourself instead of letting the observations set it: per-cell rates comparable across the map, or a resolution that stays fixed as the sample grows. Hexagons (type = "hex") avoid the axis-aligned artefacts of squares and put all six neighbours of a cell at the same distance.

Usage

create_grid_polygons(
  boundary,
  target_cells = NULL,
  type = c("square", "hex"),
  cellsize = NULL,
  n = NULL,
  clip = TRUE,
  crs = NULL,
  quiet = FALSE,
  max_cells = 1e+06
)

Arguments

boundary

Polygonal sf or sfc object, the study area the grid is laid over and clipped to. Rows without a location, rows the repair leaves without a polygon, vertices at a latitude beyond 90 and mixed dimensions are handled as "Boundaries" in spatialkit-geometry says. A boundary without a CRS that crs stamps with a geographic CRS is tested for its latitude in the same way.

target_cells

Optional approximate desired number of cells. Besides a number it accepts what approx_n_cells of build_tessellation() accepts and reads it the same way: the ranked levels of determine_optimal_levels() (the first is used), a select_resolution() result (its $best) or a resolution_profile(), with the warnings and errors described there. The cell size is derived from it as sqrt(area / target_cells), where area is that of the boundary's bounding box, so square grids get square cells; for hex grids the count is adjusted for hexagonal packing density and the size rounded so that a whole number of hexagon widths spans the longer side of the box. The size does not depend on which way the boundary lies; the count can, because hexagon rows are 0.87 cellsize apart while columns are cellsize apart (about 10 percent on a moderately elongated box, up to 1.7 times on a strip narrower than one hexagon). The count is approximate: square cells over an elongated bounding box need more cells than rectangles would (a 1000 x 1 strip at target_cells = 9 gives cells of side 10.5 and about 95 of them), and clipping to an irregular boundary moves the count again. Pass cellsize when the count matters more than the shape.

type

Grid type: "square" (the default) or "hex".

cellsize

Optional numeric cell size (length 1 or 2), in the units of the working CRS. Takes precedence over n and target_cells: if either is also supplied, cellsize is used, the other is ignored and a warning is logged. Supply exactly one of target_cells, cellsize and n. For type = "hex" a hexagon is defined by a single edge-to-edge distance, so only cellsize[1] is used and a differing cellsize[2] is ignored with a logged warning. A side of the boundary's bounding box that exceeds a whole number of square cells, of this size or of the size derived from target_cells, by no more than a margin of one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the boundary, at most a millionth of the diagonal of its bounding box and at least four times the spacing of doubles at that coordinate, gets that number of cells, so a box of 9000 by 6000 at 1000 gets 9 by 6 cells in any unit or origin, where rounding could add a row or column. A boundary so far from the origin of its coordinates that doubles there are spaced more than a millionth of its extent apart (0.125 at 1e15, beside a boundary a few kilometres across) has its grid lines rounded to that spacing; the grid is laid, and a warning of class "spatialkit_xy_imprecise" gives the spacing and the extent.

n

Optional grid resolution (integer, length 1 or 2) giving the number of columns and rows to divide the boundary's bounding box into; the cell size is derived from it. sf::st_make_grid() derives hexagon placement from cellsize alone, so for type = "hex" n does not set the number of cells, although it does change the grid, because the cellsize derived from it is what the hexagons are built with. Ignored (with a logged warning) when cellsize is also supplied. Passing both would otherwise truncate the grid to n[1] x n[2] cells anchored at the bounding-box corner, covering only part of the boundary. Wins over target_cells, which is then ignored with a logged warning.

clip

Logical; clip the grid to the boundary. Default TRUE. In a projected or CRS-less grid, a cell that meets the boundary only within a margin of the cell's edge (the margin cellsize gives: one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the boundary, within its bounds; a cell whose edge lies on the boundary's edge up to rounding) is dropped, rather than kept as a sliver. The call stops when the clip leaves no cell, as it does when the lattice has none: in degrees with s2 on, a boundary edge that spans more than 180 degrees of longitude is read as the shorter great-circle arc, the other way round the globe.

crs

Optional target CRS: anything sf::st_crs() accepts, including an sf or sfc layer, whose CRS is used. When NULL (default) a lon/lat boundary is projected with ensure_projected(), which changes the CRS of the returned grid; a message reports this unless quiet = TRUE. When that CRS would distort cell areas across the boundary by more than 1 percent (Web Mercator over a near-global extent, a UTM zone stretched well past its width), ensure_projected(purpose = "area") is used instead, with a logged warning, so the cells stay equal-area; a local extent keeps its UTM zone. A geographic crs (EPSG:4326, say) is the CRS the grid is returned in: a grid sized by target_cells or n is laid in that projected CRS and then transformed, with long edges densified. A cellsize is in the units of crs, so with a geographic crs it is in degrees and the grid is laid in degrees, as asked; such cells are not equal-area. With sf::sf_use_s2() on (the default) such a grid is clipped with sf's spherical engine s2, and s2 measures and joins its cells after; s2 refuses a polygon that is not valid on the sphere. The rows of boundary and the cells are checked with s2 whatever sf::sf_use_s2() says. Before the clip, a row of boundary that s2 refuses is repaired, with crossing edges split. A cell that lists a corner twice in a row, or two corners within 1e-12 degrees of each other, which s2 reads as one point, is returned with one of them, which moves no corner and changes the cell's area by rounding. A row of boundary, or a cell, that s2 refuses even then (a cell of a grid laid past latitude 90, say) stops the call with an error of class "spatialkit_cells_degenerate" that names its rows and s2's reason, and says to pass a projected crs or to size the grid by target_cells or n.

quiet

Logical; suppress this function's progress message()s. It does not silence R warnings, nor the package's console log echo (see spatialkit_quiet for that). Default FALSE.

max_cells

Upper bound on the number of cells the grid may have, estimated from the boundary's bounding box before anything is built. Default 1e6. A cellsize in the wrong units (metres on a boundary in kilometres, say) asks for a grid that cannot be built, and this refuses it with a message before memory is exhausted. Set to Inf to disable.

Value

An sf polygon layer with one column, poly_id, numbering the cells in the order sf::st_make_grid() lays them (row by row from the bottom left). The numbering differs from that of create_grid_polygons_cached() and ensure_stable_poly_id(), which sort cells by position; pass the result to ensure_stable_poly_id() for IDs that do not depend on how the grid was built. Use one builder throughout an analysis, since a summary keyed on the IDs of one drawn on the cells of the other puts the values on the wrong cells.

Details

Size the grid with exactly one of target_cells (roughly how many cells you want; the package derives the rest), cellsize (a fixed edge length in CRS units) or n (a fixed number of columns and rows). When more than one is given, cellsize wins over the other two and n wins over target_cells; each argument ignored is named in a logged warning.

See also

Other cell building: build_tessellation(), clip_target_for(), create_grid_polygons_cached(), create_voronoi_polygons(), ensure_stable_poly_id(), get_voronoi_seeds(), plot_tessellation_map(), voronoi_seeds_kmeans(), voronoi_seeds_random()

Examples

library(sf)
bnd <- st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(rbind(
  c(0, 0), c(100, 0), c(100, 100), c(0, 100), c(0, 0)
))), crs = 32632))
grid_sq  <- create_grid_polygons(bnd, target_cells = 100, type = "square")
grid_hex <- create_grid_polygons(bnd, target_cells = 100, type = "hex")
nrow(grid_sq)
#> [1] 100
# The hex count runs above the target: clipping keeps every hexagon that
# overhangs the boundary, and that adds more, in proportion, at a small
# target_cells.
nrow(grid_hex)
#> [1] 114
